A read-only borrowed handle to a value, or to a node inside one.
NOTICE: Value members are referenced as plain text below, not as a cref: Value is declared further down and MSVC rejects a forward reference in a doc comment (C4638, an error here).
This is what child access hands back: Value::operator[], the iterators and Value::find return a handle, which is one pointer and owns nothing.
It borrows: a handle is valid while the value it points into is alive and unmodified. Any structural change to a container invalidates the handles into it, exactly like a std::vector reference. Taking a writable handle counts as a modification even when nothing is written through it: the value may be sharing its storage with a copy of itself, and handing out write access is what forces the two apart. So do not hold a handle across a point where any writable handle to the same value is taken. Read-only handles never trigger that, and a value only ever shares with copies of itself.
A default-constructed handle, and a handle to a member that does not exist, is empty: it reads as and every write through it is ignored, so a chain like value["a"]["b"] never faults.
A converts to one implicitly, so a function that only reads should take a by value and accepts both. Use Value{handle} to take a copy where an API needs a real .
The storage of a value, and of any node inside it; the full description is with the storage bridges.
